extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional fiction writers (especially fantasy and science-fiction authors) working on magic systems and worldbuilding
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative guidelines for creating and improving magic systems and broader worldbuilding in fantasy/SF fiction, emphasizing depth, interconnectedness, and manageable complexity. Includes concrete strategies (extrapolate, interconnect, streamline) and cautions about overbuilding and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand what you already have before you add something new
rubrics_metrics.description: “Expand what you already have before you add something new.” (Sanderson’s Third Law.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core maxim: rather than continually inventing new powers, cultures, or elements, deepen and extrapolate the ramifications of the elements you already introduced. The best storytelling often comes from changing one or two things and purposefully exploring their consequences rather than having a thousand disparate powers. Anti-pattern: adding lots of different ‘cool’ abilities that don’t interrelate and make the world feel shallow or cluttered (example: sequels/crammed villains such as Spider-Man 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid worldbuilder’s disease — balance worldbuilding with core craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against “worldbuilder’s disease”: focusing heavily on worldbuilding at the expense of prose, characterization, and plotting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your goal is to be a professional novelist, practice the craft elements (prose, character, plot) as well as setting design. It’s fine to focus on setting for fun, but for strong stories prioritize narratological skills. Anti-pattern: an author who can design elaborate settings but cannot write compelling scenes or characters (you’re not a novelist if you only build settings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolate — ask “what happens when” and tailor scope to story goals
rubrics_metrics.description: “Extrapolate” — consider how the changes you’ve made will affect the world as a whole; ask ‘what happens when’ questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at social, economic, military, gender, religious, and other consequences of a magic or change, and keep scope appropriate to story length and goals (epic can explore history/economics; urban fantasy can zoom to a single cultural effect). Examples of questions: “What happens when a wizard converts to Christianity?” or “What happens to warfare if magic creates food out of thin air?” Use those consequences to generate plot and character conflict. Anti-pattern: jumbling too many unrelated powers into a tight narrative space instead of following a few powers in depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interconnect — tie powers, cultures, and themes together
rubrics_metrics.description: “Interconnect” — make powers, cultures, and themes work together rather than feeling like separate gimmicks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theme abilities toward common roles or uses (Sanderson’s Mistborn: abilities themed for a thieving crew) so the magic system feels cohesive and woven into the book’s themes. Connect magic to institutions, culture, and subthemes (e.g., industrial revolution theme helped Mistborn cohere). Benefit: makes magic feel integral rather than a grab-bag of cool tricks. Anti-pattern: disparate powers that exist only as isolated stunts; avoid giving every character an unrelated power with no thematic or practical link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamline — combine and reuse existing elements instead of multiplying new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: “Streamline” — look for places to combine cultures, magics, or characters rather than constantly adding new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a new religion could be a schism of an existing one or whether a new character could be an existing character given different perspective. Use one distinctive magic used in different cultural ways across regions instead of inventing wholly separate systems for each. Benefits: reduces complexity creep across series, tightens narrative, and forces deeper character design. Anti-patterns: over-streamlining so all cultures become identical except one trait, or funneling all growth/power into one overburdened protagonist (implausible ‘one hero with everything’). Example: Robert Jordan cutting an underused character and distributing his parts to deepen others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate magic into society, culture, ecology, economics, and everyday life
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic (and other big changes) should be shown as embedded in societal structures: culture, ecology, economics, and daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldbuilding strength comes from demonstrating how powers affect jobs, religions, social mores, warfare, caste systems, and institutions. Example: a simple ability (change skin color) could spawn religions, new occupations, social rules, and conflicts. Use these integrations to generate authentic consequences and story opportunities rather than presenting powers in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance exposition and showing — use exposition sparingly and show where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of when to explain and when to show: exposition can move the narrative or establish setting quickly, but showing typically creates more powerful scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding the right balance takes effort and varies by story. Showing a concept often requires more words but produces stronger scenes; exposition is sometimes necessary for pacing and scope. Consider story goals when deciding how much to explicate versus dramatize; this is part of deciding when to expand depth versus add breadth.
